title: The Clutter Stressing You Out Isn’t in Your Closet
author: Nir Eyal
summary: Nir Eyal argues that simplifying your closets and calendars is incomplete unless you also tidy your beliefs, since the real goal of simplicity is peace of mind. He defines beliefs as firmly held opinions open to revision, mental maps and tools rather than facts or articles of faith, so an unhelpful belief is simply the wrong tool for the job. He cites Harvard psychologist David Levari's experiments showing that people keep seeing threats after the threats have declined, and links the practice to cognitive reappraisal, which research says makes us less reactive and better able to regulate our responses. His method is to name a belief that causes stress and then answer four questions adapted from Byron Katie: is it true, can I be certain, how do I react when I believe it, and who would I be without it. The aim is not to land on one correct belief but to see a range of choices and gain space to respond calmly.
points: Beliefs are tools that can be evaluated by whether they serve your goals, not fixed facts, so you are free to discard those that do not.
Levari's research shows people keep perceiving threats after they have declined, which is why old beliefs about problems go stale unnoticed.
Cognitive reappraisal, the conscious reconsideration of a situation, makes people less reactive and better at regulating their responses.
Four questions adapted from Byron Katie give a practical way to test a belief on paper: is it true, can I be certain, how do I react, and who would I be without it.
The purpose is to open a range of perspectives and choices, not to force a single correct conclusion.
quotes: Beliefs are firmly held opinions that are open to revision based on new evidence.
They are the mental maps we create to navigate the world around us, based on the limited information we have.

Just as a carpenter might look at the job in front of her and choose to pick up a hammer, saw, or chisel, we can look at the world around us and evaluate whether our beliefs are serving our goals. When we have the wrong tool for the job, life becomes more complicated and stressful.
When problems become rare, we count more things as problems.
Simplifying your beliefs isn’t just about correcting falsehoods. It’s also about giving yourself better tools for conducting your life.

The ultimate goal of these questions isn’t to help you land on a single “correct” belief. It’s to help you unstick your thinking and see a portfolio of perspectives, a range of different choices you can choose between.
The ultimate goal of simplicity is emotional balance and space to make calmer, less constrained life decisions.
